newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Iraq-Kuwait border zone quiet, U.N. observers say.
newsitem.headline: Iraq-Kuwait border zone quiet, U.N. observers say.

text.p: The demilitarised Iraq-Kuwait border zone was quiet following U.S. missile strikes on Tuesday against targets in southern Iraq, U.N. observers said.

A spokeswoman for the U.N. Iraq-Kuwait Observer Mission (UNIKOM) deployed on the 1991 Gulf War frontier said its observers had seen no sign of reported U.S. attacks against air defence targets in southern Iraq.

The spokeswoman noted the observers' monitoring of Iraq is limited to the small area of the country that they patrol -- a 10 km (six miles)-wide strip of Iraqi territory along the 207 km (130 mile) land border.
"Everything in the DMZ (demilitarised zone) is normal, but we can't speak for the south in general," the spokeswoman said by telephone from the frontier.
"We have no information about what is going on in other areas, and we have no comment whatsoever about reported missile strikes."

The United Nations set up the demilitarised zone on the border and deployed UNIKOM along it in 1991 after Iraqi occupation forces were driven from Kuwait in the Gulf War. Iraq had invaded and annexed Kuwait in 1990.

The main job of the 245 observers is to monitor the border and ensure no military activity occurs in the demilitarised zone that straddles the frontier. The zone is five km (three miles) wide on the Kuwaiti side.
